what_it_does: Running a large language model is slow for three distinct reasons: the initial processing of the user's prompt requires enormous matrix multiplications (big multiply operations across all input tokens); loading the model's billions of stored weights from off-chip memory dominates short-prompt response time; and for long conversations, loading the cached records of past tokens (called the KV cache — the model's running memory of prior context) from memory takes most of the time for long prompts. Existing chips try to address these bottlenecks one at a time and at the level of whole numbers. MCBP attacks all three simultaneously by cracking each weight value open into its individual bits and exploiting patterns that only become visible at that finer level.
method_in_detail:
The idea. Represent a weight stored as, say, an 8-bit integer not as one number but as 8 separate one-bit "slices" stacked on top of each other. At that level, two surprising properties appear: (a) the upper bits (the most-significant bits, which carry most of the numerical value) are almost always zero — this is called bit-slice sparsity, and it reaches 65–95% in practice because trained neural-network weights follow a bell-curve distribution centered near zero; (b) when you look at a small group of rows of the weight matrix simultaneously, their bit-slice column patterns repeat, because there are only 2^m possible distinct columns for a group of m rows (the pigeonhole principle).

Computation reduction via repetitiveness (BRCR). Take m=4 rows of the weight matrix at a time. For those 4 rows, any column of bits can only be one of 16 possible patterns. Because the hidden dimension of the model (H ~ 4,000) is far larger than 16, many columns are identical. MCBP identifies the unique patterns using a Content-Addressable Memory unit (a special lookup table that finds matches in hardware very quickly), accumulates the corresponding input activations into a short vector of 16 merged sums, then reconstructs all 4 output values by a lightweight second multiply. This can reduce the number of additions by up to 12x compared to processing weights as ordinary sparse values.

Memory compression via bit sparsity (BSTC). Weights are stored in sign-magnitude format (one bit for sign, remaining bits for size). The upper bit-slice planes (bits 3–7) exhibit over 65% zeros, so MCBP compresses them with a two-state code: a zero column is stored as a single 0 bit; a non-zero column is stored as a 1-bit flag followed by the actual m-bit data. This matches the same group-size granularity as the computation step so no data reformatting is needed at runtime, achieving lossless weight compression of those planes.

KV cache prediction via progressive bit filtering (BGPP). Rather than fetching all bits of every past token's key vector to decide which ones matter for the current query, MCBP fetches only the most-significant bit first, computes a rough attention score estimate, and eliminates any key whose partial score is already too far below the running maximum to ever make the top-k cut, loading subsequent bits only for survivors. This bit-by-bit progressive filter reduces KV cache memory accesses by up to 50%.

The result. MCBP achieves 9.43x speedup and 31.1x better energy efficiency than an NVIDIA A100 GPU, and 3.2–35x better energy efficiency than the best previous purpose-built transformer accelerators.
